nameStory: The eastern tube crab gets its name from its unusual lifestyle - it lives inside the tubes of marine worms, particularly tube-building polychaete worms. The 'eastern' part distinguishes it from similar tube-dwelling crabs found on the Pacific coast. This tiny crab has found the perfect roommate arrangement, living rent-free in someone else's home!
description: The eastern tube crab is a tiny porcelain crab that's perfectly adapted for life in tight spaces. These miniature crabs are typically less than half an inch across, with a flattened, smooth shell that allows them to squeeze into narrow worm tubes. Despite being called 'crabs,' porcelain crabs are more closely related to hermit crabs and have long, feathery feeding appendages they use to filter food from the water. Their delicate appearance and smooth texture give them their 'porcelain' nickname.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Extremely small crab, usually less than half an inch wide, with a distinctly flattened, smooth carapace that feels almost glassy to the touch

idTips.label: Feeding Appendages
idTips.description: Two prominent, feathery feeding fans (maxillipeds) that they wave in the water to catch food particles - looks like tiny pom-poms

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Found inside or very near the tubes of marine worms, particularly in muddy or sandy areas where tube worms are abundant

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves with quick, darting motions and can shed legs easily if handled - the legs break off cleanly at predetermined points

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Carapace is remarkably smooth and glossy, almost ceramic-like, without the bumps or spines found on many true crabs

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's coast, particularly in muddy or sandy bottoms where tube-building marine worms create their homes. Look for them in protected bays, estuaries, and tidal flats where polychaete worms are abundant. They're most commonly found from the low tide zone down to moderate depths.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm up, beginning their breeding season. Most easily spotted during low tides when their host worm tubes are exposed.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with highest chances of observation. Adults are breeding and feeding actively in warm waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Young crabs from summer breeding may be visible.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to find as they retreat to deeper, more stable waters or deeper into worm tubes for protection.

funFact: These tiny crabs are such perfect roommates that they actually help keep their host worm's tube clean by eating debris and leftover food particles - it's like having a live-in housekeeper that never asks for payment!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with juvenile true crabs, but the feathery feeding fans are a dead giveaway - true crabs don't have these pom-pom-like appendages. Remember: if it's tiny, smooth, and waving feathers, it's a porcelain crab!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crabs,' porcelain crabs aren't true crabs at all - they're more closely related to hermit crabs and squat lobsters. The name 'porcelain' comes from their tendency to shed limbs when threatened, breaking cleanly like fragile porcelain, though the limbs can regenerate over time.
compareHints: As the only Polyonyx species in New England waters, compare it to other local porcelain crabs in the genus Petrolisthes, which are typically larger and live under rocks rather than in worm tubes. The eastern tube crab is distinguished by its smaller size, tube-dwelling lifestyle, and more elongated body shape suited for its cramped living quarters.
